author: Dante
title: The Divine Comedy: Inferno
texts: dante-italian (Italian, verse; the author's own lines)
dante-longfellow (Longfellow, verse, line for line with the Italian: same blocks and rows)
dante-temple (Carlyle's prose, the translation Auden's class learned by heart)
leads: The class learned Inferno III and V by heart (Pearce).
Terza rima: each tercet hands its middle rhyme to the next (aba bcb cdc), so the poem cannot stop; show it as a chain on the Italian.
The gate inscription of canto III: three lines beginning with the same words.
Francesca in canto V: three tercets beginning with the same word; the line about reading no further that day.
Ulysses in canto XXVI and the word folle (see webfacts.md no. 8).

author: Dante
title: The Divine Comedy: Purgatorio
leads: The class learned Purgatorio XXVIII by heart (Pearce): the earthly paradise.
Auden sets Purgatorio XVII against The Tempest (The Dyer's Hand p. 130): love as the root of every act; XVII is the middle canto of the hundred.
A simile built in two halves, "as ... so".
The shape of the mountain against the shape of Hell: seven terraces, and how the cantos are shared out.

author: Dante
title: The Divine Comedy: Paradiso
leads: The class learned Paradiso XXXIII by heart (Pearce).
The last line of the poem; each of the three parts ends on the same word.
St Bernard's prayer that opens XXXIII: a string of paradoxes.
Words Dante had to make because none existed.
The shape of the whole: 1 + 33 + 33 + 33, and the line counts.

author: Aeschylus
title: Agamemnon
texts: agamemnon (E. D. A. Morshead's verse translation, 1881; the meter and rhyme are Morshead's)
leads: No Greek is on hand; the verse shown is the translator's, and that must be said.
The watchman's opening speech.
Speakers trading single lines (stichomythia) where Clytemnestra talks Agamemnon onto the crimson cloth.
The net: one image carried through the play; count where it comes.
Cassandra.

author: Sophocles
title: Antigone
texts: antigone (F. Storr's verse translation, 1912; the verse is Storr's)
leads: No Greek is on hand.
Antigone and Creon, or Creon and Haemon, trading single lines: an argument drawn as a duel, line against line.
The chorus on man, "many wonders".
Auden changed his mind about this play; the notes give both views.

author: Horace
title: Odes
texts: horace-la (Latin, verse; the author's own lines)
leads: Latin can put words in almost any order. Show an ode where adjectives and their nouns are wound round one another (the Pyrrha ode, I.5; the Soracte ode, I.9), with the English beside it.
Meter by long and short syllables: one stanza of an Alcaic or Sapphic ode.
Carpe diem (I.11) and the monument ode (III.30).
Auden wrote syllabic verse on these models.

author: Augustine
title: Confessions
leads: The whole book is spoken to God: apostrophe as the form of a book.
The opening paragraph and its restless heart.
The pear tree (book 2).
The garden and the child's voice (book 8).
"Too late loved I thee" (book 10): repetition and antithesis.
How the words of the Psalms are woven into his own sentences.

author: Shakespeare
title: Henry IV, Part 2
leads: Who speaks verse and who speaks prose, scene by scene: count it.
The King on sleep (3.1).
The rejection of Falstaff (5.5): the new king's verse against Falstaff's prose.
Auden on Falstaff, in the 1941 class and later ("The Prince's Dog").

author: Shakespeare
title: Othello
leads: Othello's own music against Iago's speech, and how Othello's verse breaks when Iago has done his work.
One line that says the same words twice with two meanings (5.2).
Iago in verse and in prose.
Auden on Iago, in the 1941 class and in "The Joker in the Pack".

author: Shakespeare
title: Hamlet
leads: Hendiadys, one idea said through two nouns joined by "and": the play is full of it. Count some.
The soliloquy of 3.1: lines with an extra syllable at the end, a run of infinitives.
Hamlet's prose.
Auden thought the play a problem; see the notes.

author: Shakespeare
title: The Tempest
scope: The whole play. The first plate, Ariel's song, is done: it is the model. Add at most two more plates from elsewhere in the play and leave the first as it is.
leads: Caliban on the island's noises (3.2).
Prospero's revels speech (4.1) or his farewell to his art (5.1).
The epilogue: the same four-beat line as the spirits' songs, now spoken by Prospero.
Auden: "one cannot possibly like him" (The Dyer's Hand pp. 128-29); the parallel with The Magic Flute.

author: Ben Jonson
title: Volpone
leads: Volpone's morning speech to his gold (1.1): the words of worship turned on money.
The names: each character is a beast or bird of prey. The cast as a diagram of who feeds on whom.
Jonson's verse against Shakespeare's.
Auden on Jonson's comedy (The Dyer's Hand).

author: Pascal
title: Pensées
leads: The wager: an argument that can be drawn as a table of four outcomes.
The thinking reed; the silence of the infinite spaces: sentences built on antithesis.
A book of fragments: what the unfinished form does.
Baudelaire and Pascal's abyss.

author: Racine
title: Phèdre
texts: .cache/originals/racine_phedre_fr_wikisource.txt (French, the author's own lines; bring a passage in with original.mjs)
leads: The French twelve-syllable line, cut in the middle after the sixth: a balance of two halves, and couplets in pairs. Show it on the French with Boswell beside it.
The line made of two proper names (1.1).
Phèdre's first account of her love (1.3) or the declaration (2.5).
How few different words Racine uses.

author: Blake
title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
leads: The Proverbs of Hell: each a sentence in two halves set against each other.
The Argument that opens the book.
Contraries: the book's own word for its method.
Auden took a title from this book (The Prolific and the Devourer) and cited Blake in the 1941 Tempest lecture.

author: Goethe
title: Faust, Part I
texts: .cache/originals/faust_german.txt (German, the author's own lines; bring a passage in with original.mjs)
faust (Bayard Taylor's translation in the original meters, 1870)
leads: Goethe changes meter with the speaker and the mood. Faust's first speech in the rough four-beat line of old German popular verse; the archangels' hymn; Gretchen at the spinning wheel in two-beat lines with a returning stanza.
A map of which scene is in which meter.
Mephistopheles naming himself.

author: Kierkegaard
title: Fear and Trembling
scope: Hollander's selections (about a third of the book).
research: C section 15, and the lecture in appendix H21
leads: The story of Abraham and Isaac told four ways, each ending with the same turn about weaning a child: set the four side by side and mark what changes.
Check that the four tellings are in Hollander's selection.
Auden's Kierkegaard lecture of October 1941 (Pearce).

author: Baudelaire
title: Intimate Journals
scope: Rockets and My Heart Laid Bare.
leads: Notes to himself: the sentence as a blow. Antithesis and paradox.
The rules of hygiene, conduct and method: a list of resolutions.
The dandy.
Auden's introduction of 1947.

author: Ibsen
title: Peer Gynt
texts: peer-gynt (William and Charles Archer's verse translation; the verse is the Archers', after Ibsen's meters)
leads: The onion (act 5): one figure carried through a whole speech, layer by layer, each layer a part Peer has played. Map each layer to the earlier scene it names.
The trolls' motto against the human one: one word differs.
The Button-Moulder.
Auden on Peer Gynt ("Genius and Apostle" in The Dyer's Hand).

author: Dostoevsky
title: The Brothers Karamazov
leads: The Grand Inquisitor (book 5, chapter 5): a speaker inside a speaker inside a narrator, and a listener who never answers. Draw who is speaking.
The three temptations as the plan of the speech.
The kiss.
What Auden said; the notes say what was found.

author: Rimbaud
title: Une Saison en Enfer
texts: rimbaud (the English version printed in The Dial, 1920)
leads: Prose that keeps breaking into exclamation and fragment: sentence length drawn out along a page.
"Alchemy of the Word": he quotes his own verse and passes judgment on it.
The last section, "Adieu".
Set the French beside the English and mark what the translator did.

author: Henry Adams
title: The Education of Henry Adams
leads: A life of himself written as "he": what the third person does, sentence by sentence.
The Dynamo and the Virgin (chapter 25): two forces set level.
The long sentence that ends in a deflation.

author: Melville
title: Moby-Dick
leads: Ahab's speeches are prose that scans as blank verse (chapter 37, "Sunset"; chapter 132, "The Symphony"): set a passage as lines and scan it.
The 135 chapters by kind: story, play with stage directions, the science of whales, sermon. Count them.
The first sentence.
Auden on Ahab (The Enchafèd Flood; "The Christian Tragic Hero").
scans: ef.txt is The Enchafèd Flood, much of it on this book

author: Rilke
title: The Journal of My Other Self
scope: The whole book (The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge).
texts: rilke (M. D. Herter Norton and John Linton's translation, 1930; prose)
rilke-de and poems (two poems, German and English: Herbsttag, Der Panther)
leads: "I am learning to see."
The passage on what a single line of verse costs: one long sentence built on the same opening words, then the turn.
One of the two poems in German with the English beside it, if it serves the book.

author: Kafka
title: The Castle
texts: castle (Willa and Edwin Muir's translation, 1930; prose)
leads: The first paragraph: a castle that is said to be there by saying what cannot be seen.
A sentence that takes back what it has just given: draw the clauses.
Klamm's letter and K.'s two readings of it.
Auden, "K.'s Quest".

author: T. S. Eliot
title: The Family Reunion
scope: The whole play. IN COPYRIGHT: no text is hosted and none may be shown.
leads: Nothing of the play may be printed beyond two quotations of at most 25 words. The piece is a "shape" plate (noText): the verse line Eliot made for it, as he later described it himself; who speaks as a chorus; the Greek play under it.
Verify Eliot's own account of the line (in "Poetry and Drama", 1951) before using it, and cite it.
What Auden said of the play.

author: Gluck
title: Orpheus
texts: orpheus (the English of a libretto translated by Manfredo Maggioni)
.cache/originals/gluck_orfeo_ed_euridice_it_ricordi_1879_ia_ocr.txt (Italian, raw OCR: check each line you use)
leads: The aria of the last act, where he has lost her a second time: a lament in a major key. Its words come round three times with two episodes between.
The Italian eight-syllable line.
Hanslick's remark on this aria (webfacts.md no. 5: note the correction there).
record: site/records/orpheus-che-faro-onegin-1922.mp3: Sigrid Onegin singing this aria, about 1922; the piece may offer it to hear the words sung

author: Mozart
title: Don Giovanni
leads: The duet in which Giovanni wins Zerlina: he sings a stanza, she answers in the same form, then the lines shorten and their voices close up until they share a line. The form is the seduction.
Leporello's catalogue: a list with numbers.
Auden on Don Giovanni and Tristan as the two myths of love.

author: Mozart
title: The Magic Flute
leads: The Queen of the Night's second aria: a mother's curse in strict verse.
Who is good and who is bad changes between the acts: the plan of the opera.
Speech against song.
Auden later translated this libretto and wrote on it; he set it beside The Tempest.

author: Beethoven
title: Fidelio
texts: fidelio (English libretto; mostly spoken prose with sung numbers)
leads: Leonore's great scene: fury, then hope.
Speech, song, and speech over music in the dungeon: what is said in each.
Auden set her answer to Florestan beside Cordelia's answer to the waking Lear, Act 4, Scene 7 (appendix H16; the lecture's text gives Leonore's word twice, the uncut German once).

author: Wagner
title: The Flying Dutchman
leads: Senta's ballad: a ballad sung inside the opera, three stanzas and a refrain, and she breaks the form at the end to step into the story.
Wagner still writing in rhyme here; compare what he did later.

author: Wagner
title: Tristan und Isolde
leads: Isolde's last song: questions that are never answered, short lines, one long climb.
In act 2 the lovers talk about the word "and" in their two names: grammar as the subject.
Wagner's short line with alliteration and rhyme together.
Auden lectured on Tristan in the 1941 class (it was assigned with Carmen).

author: Wagner
title: Götterdämmerung
leads: Wagner gave up rhyme at the line end and bound his lines by alliteration, as old Germanic verse did. Show the German with its chiming stressed syllables, and how the translator kept it.
The Norns, or Brünnhilde's last scene.
The record on hand is the funeral march, which has no words.

author: Bizet
title: Carmen
scope: The libretto, by Meilhac and Halévy.
leads: The Habanera: Carmen states her law of love as a song, in couplets with a refrain; the grammar is "if you ... I", a condition and a threat.
What Auden said; it was assigned with Tristan.

author: Verdi
title: La Traviata
leads: Violetta alone at the end of act 1: a slow song of doubt, then a fast one of defiance, with Alfredo's voice from outside between. The set form of an Italian scene, and what she does with it.
Italian verse in libretti: lines that end on a stressed syllable close a stanza.
